meta.title: Who really said "They Riot in the Streets Inflamed with Wild Notions; Their Morals Are Decaying"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Plato. The complaint about rioting youth is traced no further back than a 1967 Notre Dame commencement address — 2,300 years short of its billing.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'They Riot in the Streets Inflamed with Wild Notions; Their Morals Are Decaying'?
meta.ogDescription: The most-quoted thing Plato never wrote. Earliest known appearance: June 1967, already labelled “Plato, 427–347 B.C.”

answer.label: Not Plato — traced no further back than 1967
answer.authorDates: First documented 12 June 1967 · no author has ever been identified
answer.sourceLine: Plato did not write this. Quote Investigator has found no substantive evidence for him ↗, and the earliest instance it can locate is only from 1967 — when Theodore M. Hesburgh, then president of the University of Notre Dame, opened a commencement address at Manchester College in Indiana by reading it out already attributed to “Plato (427-347 B.C.)”. So Hesburgh is not the author either: QI’s view is that he probably saw an earlier printed instance somewhere, though where is not certain. From there it passed to a newspaper editors’ convention in 1968, to a Supreme Court justice, to the Congressional Record, and to Isaac Asimov’s Book of Facts. Nobody along that chain produced a source, because there is no Greek original to produce.

source.excerpt: I would like to begin this morning by quoting to you something that may sound familiar: “What is happening to our young people? They disrespect their elders. They disobey their parents. They ignore the laws. They riot in the streets inflamed with wild notions. Their morals are decaying. What is to become of them?” Plato (427-347 B.C.) Those words were written originally in Greek, by Plato, about 400 years before the birth of Christ.
source.trailTitle: How a 1967 quotation became 2,300 years old
trail: June 1967 — the earliest instance. Hesburgh’s Manchester College commencement address, printed in the Notre Dame pamphlet Thoughts IV (1968), quote page 29 — verified with scans by QI ↗, which added this citation to its article in August 2021. The passage is already credited to Plato, with dates.

April 1968 — and it is already drifting. At the American Society of Newspaper Editors convention in Washington, the panel moderator Creed C. Black of The Chicago Daily News used it to open a session titled “What about the Generation Gap?” (quote page 105). His version reads “they ride in the streets inflamed with wild notions. Their morals are decayed” — which QI suggests may reflect an imperfect transcription of the speech ↗. Two words had already moved within a year.

June 1968 — the Supreme Court. Justice William J. Brennan Jr. delivered “A Judge Looks at Student Dissent” at Harvard, published in the Harvard Law School Bulletin that July (quote page 9). He introduced the passage as “a complaint by Plato, some 2300 years ago” — in QI’s citations ↗. Twelve months after Hesburgh’s address, the line was being read out by a sitting justice of the Supreme Court — still with no source.

1968–1969 — into the record. A Pittsburgh Press letter to the editor ran it on 29 July 1968 signed “–Plato 427-437 B.C.” (the dates mistyped); the San Diego Union carried it in a Christmas-letter column that December; a Sarasota columnist noted in January 1969 that congressmen had taken to inserting it in the Congressional Record; and on 17 July 1969 Representative John Brademas of Indiana did exactly that, with a Hesburgh address titled “In Defense of the Younger Generation” (quote page 19992) — all dated and paginated by QI ↗.

1979 — and into the reference shelf. Isaac Asimov’s Book of Facts printed it under “Ancient Peoples” (quote page 35) with the preface “And Plato wrote of his students”. To Asimov’s credit, the book opens by conceding that “I may have let a non-fact or two get by me” — QI quotes both ↗. The line is also absent from Wikiquote’s Plato page ↗, including its Misattributed section.
source.excerptNote: The oldest appearance anyone has found, as Quote Investigator transcribes it from scans of the 1968 pamphlet ↗. Read what it actually shows: Hesburgh is quoting, not composing — “something that may sound familiar” — and the Plato label with its dates is already attached. The trail does not begin with an invention; it begins with a man repeating something he had read somewhere, and QI says plainly that where he read it is not known.
source.rightsHolder: The University of Notre Dame (the 1968 pamphlet) and the estate of Theodore M. Hesburgh
source.rightsNote: There is no ancient Greek original here, so nothing about this passage is public-domain by age. The oldest text it can be traced to is Hesburgh’s 1967 address as printed in a University of Notre Dame pamphlet in 1968 — well after the pre-1931 cutoff for automatic US public domain — and the title-case wording displayed at the top of this page is Quote Investigator’s own 2014 article heading. Treat the passage as modern, in-copyright text of unidentified authorship, and do not reuse it as a Plato quotation at all.

author.name: Plato
author.kicker: The man who got the credit
author.heading: So what did Plato actually say about the young?
author.metaLine: c. 428–347 BC · Athenian philosopher, founder of the Academy
author.bio: Plato is the foundational thinker of the Western philosophical tradition — student of Socrates, teacher of Aristotle, founder of the Academy at Athens, and author of the dialogues that gave us the Theory of Forms. He did write about undisciplined young men, and the real passage is sharper than the forgery: at Republic 555c he argues that rulers who hold power because they own a great deal will not pass laws stopping undisciplined young people from squandering their wealth, precisely because lending to them against their property and then calling the loans in is how those rulers grow richer still. That is a complaint about the old exploiting the young, which is close to the opposite of the line on this page. Being a magnet for invented aphorisms is an occupational hazard of his standing: Wikiquote’s Plato page carries a Misattributed section listing eight other sayings handed to him ↗, from “Only the dead have seen the end of war” to “Be kind, for everyone you meet is fighting a hard battle”.

misattribution.heading: A fabrication with a 2,300-year alibi
misattribution.intro: The attraction of this passage is that it appears to prove the generation gap is eternal. That is also why nobody checked it: a quotation whose whole point is its age is the last thing anyone asks for a page number.

items.why: Quote Investigator “has found no substantive evidence that Plato made the statement” ↗ and concludes that it has “only been traced back to 1967”. No dialogue, letter or fragment has ever been cited for it, and it does not appear on Wikiquote’s Plato page ↗ — not among the sourced quotations and not in its Misattributed section, which does list eight other things he never said.

Hesburgh’s June 1967 address is the oldest instance located, but he introduced it as “something that may sound familiar” with the Plato credit already attached, and QI believes he probably saw an earlier published instance, while stating that where he obtained it is not certain ↗. He was president of Notre Dame for thirty-five years and chaired the US Commission on Civil Rights ↗ — a man defending the young, using what he took to be a classical parallel.

items.who: Creed C. Black, William J. Brennan Jr. and the Congressional Record
items.why: A newspaper-editors’ panel (April 1968), a Supreme Court justice at Harvard (June 1968) and the Congressional Record (July 1969) each passed it on as Plato’s — all three documented by QI ↗. None cited a text. Each repetition by a more eminent speaker made the next one likelier, which is the entire mechanism by which an unsourced quotation becomes common knowledge.

The other famous ancient complaint about young people — usually given to Socrates — was traced by QI to Kenneth John Freeman’s 1907 Cambridge dissertation ↗, where it was Freeman’s own summary of ancient grievances rather than a quotation of anybody. The New York Times retracted it. Two of the best-known proofs that “nothing changes” are both twentieth-century compositions.

misattribution.truthLine: Nobody knows who wrote it. Quote Investigator’s conclusion: “QI has not yet found any substantive citations for Plato. The words have only been traced back to 1967, but the provenance remains mysterious.” ↗

context.heading: Why this one was never checked
lead: The passage surfaced in the summer of 1967 and spread through 1968 — which is to say, into the single most convulsive stretch of American campus and street protest of the century. It said exactly what a great many people wanted said, and it said it with the authority of antiquity: if Plato complained about rioting youth, then the present disorder was not a crisis of the republic but a permanent feature of being young.

That is also precisely why it survived unexamined for half a century. A quotation offered as evidence that nothing ever changes is self-insulating — checking it would defeat its only purpose. And it travelled upward rather than sideways: Hesburgh to a newspaper editors’ panel, to a Supreme Court justice, to the Congressional Record, to a popular book of facts. Plato ↗ has borne it ever since.
context.detailsSummary: The giveaway is in the wording
detailsBody: Hesburgh told his audience the words “were written originally in Greek, by Plato”. A translated passage ought to vary between renderings — different translators, different English. This one does not: every instance from 1967 onward repeats the same seven short English clauses in the same order, which is the signature of a text copied in English rather than translated from Greek.

The two variations that do appear are transmission noise, not translation. The 1968 newspaper-editors version has “ride in the streets” for “riot” and “morals are decayed” for “decaying”, which QI suggests reflects imperfect transcription of a spoken address ↗. A letter in the Pittsburgh Press managed to mistype Plato’s own dates as “427-437 B.C.” Nobody was consulting a source; they were copying each other.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator states it has found no substantive evidence that Plato made the statement; that the earliest instance it located is in the pamphlet Thoughts IV: Five Addresses Delivered During 1967 by Theodore M. Hesburgh, in the speech "Service: The Great Modern Prayer" given at the Manchester College commencement, North Manchester, Indiana, on June 12, 1967, quote page 29, published 1968 by the University of Notre Dame and verified with scans from archive.org; that QI believes Hesburgh probably saw an earlier published instance but where he obtained it is not certain; that the next instances are the April 1968 ASNE convention panel moderated by Creed C. Black (quote page 105, with "ride in the streets" and "morals are decayed"), William J. Brennan Jr.’s June 1968 Harvard speech in the Harvard Law School Bulletin (quote page 9, "a complaint by Plato, some 2300 years ago"), a Pittsburgh Press letter of 29 July 1968 signed "Plato 427-437 B.C.", the San Diego Union of 31 December 1968, a Sarasota Journal column of 23 January 1969, the Congressional Record of 17 July 1969 (quote page 19992, inserted by Congressman John Brademas of Indiana, Hesburgh’s "In Defense of the Younger Generation"), and Isaac Asimov’s Book of Facts (quote page 35, "And Plato wrote of his students"), with Asimov’s own caveat that "I may have let a non-fact or two get by me"; and that QI concludes the words have only been traced back to 1967 and the provenance remains mysterious.

Quote Investigator traces "The children now love luxury. They have bad manners, contempt for authority; they show disrespect for elders and love chatter in place of exercise" — usually attributed to Socrates — to Kenneth John Freeman’s Cambridge dissertation published in 1907, where Freeman was presenting his own summary of ancient complaints rather than quoting anyone, and notes the New York Times retracted the quote with a note that many researchers agree Plato is not the source.

Wikiquote’s Plato page does not contain this passage anywhere, including in its Misattributed section, which lists eight other sayings wrongly attributed to Plato — among them "Only the dead have seen the end of war", "Be kind, for everyone you meet is fighting a hard battle" and "Music is a moral law". The page also carries, from the Republic, the sourced passage about rulers unwilling to enact laws preventing undisciplined young people from wasting their wealth so that the rulers may grow richer by lending to them.

Wikipedia states Plato lived c. 428–347 BC, was an ancient Greek philosopher of Classical Athens considered the foundational thinker of the Western philosophical tradition, founded the Academy in Athens, and is most famous for the Theory of Forms; his teacher was Socrates and his student Aristotle.

Wikipedia states Theodore Martin Hesburgh, C.S.C. lived May 25, 1917 – February 26, 2015, was an American Catholic priest of the Congregation of Holy Cross, served as president of the University of Notre Dame for 35 years from 1952 to 1987, chaired the United States Commission on Civil Rights, and received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1964 and the Congressional Gold Medal in 2000.
